To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ETS has induced CO2 reductions in Germany which are too small and that a unilateral flexible cap is a promising instrument to improve the EU ETS.

the EU ETS is not effective in reducing CO2 emissions in electricity sector, that the EU E TS should be decoupled from the promotion of renewables and that a unilateral flexible cap could be a promising instrument to eliminate demand side effect.
the EU ETS is sub-optimal and a unilateral flexible cap is a remedy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a unilateral flexible cap for the German electricity sector and with its implications for the EU ETS as a whole.
the design and implementation of a flexible cap in the German electricity industry.
the design of an optimal emission cap for the German electricity sector and its impact on the EU ETS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EU ETS has not contributed to a significant reduction in German CO2 emissions in 2008–12.
a unilateral flexible cap in the electricity sector is a promising instrument for improving the performance of the EU-ETS.
the EU ETS is not the right policy instrument to reduce CO2 emissions in electricity sector.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a unilateral flexible cap could be a useful instrument to decouple the EU ETS in the electricity sector from excessive allowances and from subsidized renewable energy.
a flexible cap is a promising instrument to improve the EU ETS and to decouple it from other policies.
the EU ETS is not a good instrument to promote renewables.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a flexible cap is a promising tool to eliminate demand side impacts and to decouple the EU ETS.
a flexible intensity cap is a promising tool to improve the EU ETS.
a flexible cap can improve the performance of an emissions trading system.
